## [00:00] Introduction to Natural Language Processing Challenges

**Spoken content:** Natural language presents many unique challenges compared to other data types like images and structured data, requiring a different approach. Today, we'll explore a foundational concept for modeling natural language called "bag of words." We'll discuss what it means and how to use it for text processing.

**On-screen content:**
![Yufeng Guo speaking in front of a white background, wearing a grey t-shirt with the Google Cloud logo](video-frame://25@00:00)

## [00:29] AI Adventures: Getting Started with Natural Language Processing: Bag of Words

**Spoken content:** Welcome to AI Adventures, where we explore the art, science, and tools of machine learning. My name is Yufeng Guo, and in this episode, we'll look at how to use bag of words to classify natural language.

**On-screen content:**
![Title card: AI Adventures, Getting started with Natural Language Processing: Bag of words, Yufeng Guo @YufengG](video-frame://25@00:29)

## [00:46] The Special Nature of Natural Language

**Spoken content:** Natural language is special because it has inherent structure while also being very free-form. There are many ways to express the same idea, and similar words can convey very different meanings.

**On-screen content:**
![Slide: Natural language. Examples of sentences with subtle differences in meaning based on word choice or emphasis, such as "I never said my dog ate my homework." and "What were you thinking? 🤨 What were you thinking? 🤯"](video-frame://25@00:46)

## [01:03] Converting Data to Matrices

**Spoken content:** In machine learning, we often convert data into matrices or tensors. This is straightforward for images, as they already have an inherent matrix representation (e.g., RGB channels). Structured data also easily maps to input matrix values. However, for natural language, we need a method to transform words into numbers so they can be used in these matrices.

**On-screen content:**
![Slide: Data -> Matrices. An image of a cat is shown with its Red, Green, and Blue color channels represented as matrices of numbers.](video-frame://25@01:03)

## [01:29] Bag of Words: Encoding Free-Form Text

**Spoken content:** There are many ways to convert text into numerical representations. Today, we'll focus on an approach called "bag of words."

**On-screen content:**
![Slide: Bag of words: encoding free form text. A cloth bag filled with Scrabble tiles is shown.](video-frame://25@01:29)

## [01:39] Understanding Bag of Words with a Vocabulary Example

**Spoken content:** Let's imagine we're learning English for the first time, and our initial vocabulary consists of these ten words. We want to identify if a given text is about pandas, Keras, or Matplotlib.

**On-screen content:**
![Slide: Bag of words: Vocabulary. A list of 10 words: dataframe, layer, series, graph, column, plot, color, axes, read_csv, activation.](video-frame://25@01:39)
![Slide: Bag of words: Vocabulary and Possible labels. The vocabulary list is on the left, and a list of possible labels (pandas, keras, matplotlib) is on the right.](video-frame://25@02:04)

## [02:10] Processing an Input Sentence with Bag of Words

**Spoken content:** How would we do this? If we encounter a sentence like "how to plot dataframe bar graph," we would only recognize the words "plot," "dataframe," and "graph" from our vocabulary. The rest would be ignored as gibberish. Even with just these three words, we can still get a sense of the sentence's topic.

**On-screen content:**
![Slide: Bag of words: Inputs and Vocabulary. An input sentence "how to plot dataframe bar graph" is shown. The vocabulary list is on the right.](video-frame://25@02:10)

## [02:35] Encoding the Sentence into an Array

**Spoken content:** To capture this information in an array or matrix, we create an array representing our entire vocabulary (in this case, length 10). We set all values to zero and then turn on (set to one) the indices corresponding to the words found in the input sentence. This process disregards the order of words in the input sentence, but depends on the order in our vocabulary list. This effectively "scrambles" the words, much like a bag of words.

**On-screen content:**
![Slide: Bag of words: Inputs and Vocabulary. The input sentence "how to plot dataframe bar graph" is shown with arrows pointing to the corresponding words in the vocabulary list (dataframe, plot, graph). Below, a binary array `[1 0 0 1 0 0 1 0 0 0]` represents the presence of these words in the vocabulary.](video-frame://25@02:48)

## [03:29] Preprocessing Labels for Prediction

**Spoken content:** We apply a similar preprocessing step to our labels. This is simpler as there are only three labels. For sentences that might have multiple relevant labels, we set all corresponding indices to one, leaving the rest as zero, just as we did for the words in our training data.

**On-screen content:**
![Slide: Preprocessing labels. The input sentence and its encoded array are shown on the left. On the right, "Prediction" shows the labels `[pandas keras matplotlib]` and an encoded array `[1 0 1]`, indicating that "pandas" and "matplotlib" are relevant.](video-frame://25@03:29)

## [03:55] Inputs to Predictions: Machine Learning in Action

**Spoken content:** Now that both inputs and outputs (which were originally words) are transformed into arrays of numbers, machine learning can do what it does best: map one set of numbers to another. The heavy lifting is in the preprocessing, where we encode the text into numerical representations. Bag of words is a simple approach for this task, and it can be surprisingly effective in many situations.

**On-screen content:**
![Slide: Inputs to predictions. A matrix multiplication and addition operation is shown: `[1 2; 3 4] * [2 0; 1 2] + [4 3; 0 1] = [8 7; 10 9]`. Below, `inputs [1 0 0 1 0 0 1 0 0 0]` and `prediction [1 0 1]` are displayed.](video-frame://25@03:55)

## [04:28] Encoding Text with Keras

**Spoken content:** To build a bag of words model with code, Keras offers a convenient preprocessing library. Using the `Tokenizer` class, we can select the vocabulary size. While our example used 10 words, in code, we might choose a larger number like 400. This tokenizer is then fitted on the entire training text to select the most common words.

**On-screen content:**
![Code snippet: Encoding text with Keras.
```python
tokenize = keras.preprocessing.text.Tokenizer(num_words=400)
tokenize.fit_on_texts(train_questions)

body_train = tokenize.texts_to_matrix(train_questions)
body_test = tokenize.texts_to_matrix(test_questions)
```
](video-frame://25@04:28)

## [05:00] Model Architecture for Bag of Words

**Spoken content:** Once tokenization is complete, building the model is straightforward, similar to working with other structured data. Since each row is now an input of ones and zeros, a standard fully connected deep neural network can be quite effective. For multi-label classification, where more than one label can be true for a single input, use a sigmoid activation function instead of Softmax, and pair it with binary cross-entropy loss.

**On-screen content:**
![Code snippet: Model architecture.
```python
model = keras.models.Sequential()
model.add(keras.layers.Dense(50, input_shape=(vocab_size,), activation='relu'))
model.add(keras.layers.Dense(25, activation='relu'))
model.add(keras.layers.Dense(5, activation='sigmoid'))

model.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy', optimizer='adam', metrics=['accuracy'])
```
The 'sigmoid' activation is highlighted.](video-frame://25@05:00)

## [05:36] Conclusion and Further Resources

**Spoken content:** That's the bag of words model in a nutshell. Understanding its workings, advantages, and drawbacks is crucial for building your foundation in natural language processing, especially as you move to more advanced text encoding approaches. For more details and examples, check out the expanded blog post linked in the description. Thanks for watching this episode of Cloud AI Adventures. If you enjoyed it, please like and subscribe. To continue your NLP journey, explore the TensorFlow word embedding tutorial linked below.

**On-screen content:**
![Yufeng Guo speaking in front of a white background, wearing a grey t-shirt with the Google Cloud logo.](video-frame://25@05:36)
![Slide: Yufeng Guo @YufengG. Google Cloud logo.](video-frame://25@05:57)
![Slide: Looking for more tips on ML? Watch more. Google Cloud logo.](video-frame://25@06:15)
